question: How does Java's Comparator demonstrate the Strategy pattern?
title: Comparator as Strategy Pattern in Java
direct_answer: `Comparator<T>` is a Strategy for ordering two `T` values. Sorting APIs accept that behavior as an argument, so the same data can be ordered by name, price, or date without changing its class. The comparator does not choose or represent the sorting algorithm itself; different Java APIs and data types may use different sort implementations.

sections.title: Comparator as Built-In Strategy Pattern
sections.content:
`Comparator<T>` is a small, familiar Strategy example. Its `compare(a, b)` method defines an ordering rule, and APIs such as `List.sort` or `Stream.sorted` receive that rule from the caller.

The context is the operation that needs ordering; the comparator is the interchangeable behavior. A product list can use one comparator for price and another for name without adding ordering branches to `Product`.

Do not confuse the comparison rule with the sorting algorithm. The Java API is free to use different implementations depending on the method, data representation, or parallel execution. Comparator controls how two elements are ordered, not how the overall sort is performed.

sections.title: Without Comparator-as-strategy — sort logic hardcoded
With Comparator — algorithm fixed, comparison rule injected
Comparator = Strategy, Mapped to the Pattern's Roles
sections.content:
amber|Strategy contract|~Comparator<T>|compare two values|negative zero or positive|ordering rules matter
blue|Concrete rules|~interchangeable behavior|byPrice byName byStock|lambdas work|compose with thenComparing
emerald|Context|~sorting operation|accepts a Comparator|calls it for ordering|sort implementation may vary
violet|Boundary|~not the sort algorithm|API and data type choose implementation|comparator supplies order|null policy must be explicit

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling Comparator the sorting algorithm**: it supplies pairwise ordering; the sorting API chooses its implementation.
- **Breaking the contract**: inconsistent, non-transitive comparisons can produce wrong results or runtime failures.
- **Subtracting numeric fields**: `a - b` may overflow; use `Integer.compare`, `Long.compare`, or comparator helpers.
- **Forgetting null policy**: use `nullsFirst` or `nullsLast` when null is allowed.
- **Ignoring composition**: `thenComparing` and `reversed` are clearer than duplicated branching.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `Comparator<T>` encapsulates one ordering rule
- Sorting APIs accept it as interchangeable behavior
- The same objects can be ordered in several ways without changing their class
- Comparator is the comparison strategy, not the sorting algorithm
- Comparators must satisfy their ordering contract for sorting results to be reliable

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `Comparator<T>` demonstrates Strategy because it packages one ordering rule behind a common interface. A sorting operation receives the comparator and calls `compare` without knowing whether the rule uses price, name, or date. I can pass a different comparator for the same list, compose rules with `thenComparing`, or use a lambda, while the sorting API remains unchanged. The comparator is not the sorting algorithm itself; Java may use different sort implementations for different APIs and data types. It only defines the relative order and must obey the comparator contract.

question: What is the Strategy pattern and what problem does it solve?
title: Strategy Pattern Explained
direct_answer: Strategy is a behavioral pattern that represents interchangeable behavior behind a common interface and gives a context one of those implementations through composition. It helps when an operation has several meaningful variants that should change independently. Selection still exists—often in configuration, a factory, or a registry—and a simple conditional may remain clearer for a small stable case.

sections.title: Strategy Pattern Fundamentals
sections.content:
The **Strategy pattern** represents a family of related behaviors behind one contract. A context holds the contract and delegates the operation to the implementation it receives. For example, a cart can apply a `DiscountPolicy` without containing every discount formula.

Strategy moves provider-specific or algorithm-specific code out of a growing conditional in the context. The choice does not disappear; another boundary still chooses the implementation, perhaps through configuration, a registry, a factory, or dependency injection.

The benefit is independent change and testing of each behavior. The cost is extra types and a selection mechanism. Use a lambda or simple branch when the variation is small and stable, and do not force behaviors with different contracts into one weak interface.

sections.title: Without Strategy — the if-else chain that grows forever
With Strategy — one class per algorithm, context stays closed
Strategy Pattern at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Strategy interface|~The shared contract|usually one method|e.g. apply(price)|enables substitution
blue|Concrete strategies|~One class per algorithm|NoDiscount, StudentDiscount|isolated and unit-testable|add new = add class
emerald|Context|~Holds and delegates|has-a strategy|never checks the type|stays closed for change
violet|Selection|~Happens outside|factory or Spring DI|chosen at runtime|keep it out of the context

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using Strategy for one tiny stable branch**: the added interface and selection code may be harder to read.
- **Hiding a large switch in another class**: selection remains a design responsibility even when behavior is separated.
- **Forcing unlike workflows into one interface**: the common contract should represent real substitutability.
- **Assuming the context can never know a type**: the useful boundary depends on ownership and change, not a slogan.
- **Creating stateful shared strategies without a concurrency plan**: lifecycle and thread safety still matter.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Strategy places interchangeable behavior behind one contract
- A context composes and delegates to a strategy
- Selection moves to a deliberate boundary; it does not disappear
- Each behavior can change and be tested independently
- A small conditional or lambda can be clearer for a simple stable case

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Strategy is a behavioral pattern that puts interchangeable behavior behind one interface and gives a context one implementation through composition. A cart, for example, can delegate to a `DiscountPolicy` rather than contain every discount formula. This separates the stable checkout flow from rules that change independently and makes each rule easier to test. The selection still has to happen somewhere, such as configuration, a registry, a factory, or dependency injection. I use Strategy when the variants share a real contract and are likely to grow or change. For one small stable branch, a conditional or lambda may be clearer than several new classes.

question: How do you implement Strategy pattern for a payment system in Java?
title: Strategy Pattern: Payment System Implementation
direct_answer: Define a `PaymentStrategy` contract and implement the payment behaviors that genuinely share it. A checkout service receives or selects a strategy through a small registry, factory, or injected map and delegates the payment operation. Keep provider-specific validation and results behind the contract, but do not force unlike workflows into one weak interface merely to remove every conditional.

sections.title: Building a Payment Strategy System
sections.content:
A payment example can use Strategy when several payment methods share a meaningful operation and can be selected independently of checkout. `PaymentStrategy` defines the required request and result, while card, UPI, and another provider implement their own validation and integration.

The checkout workflow delegates through the interface. Selection can happen in a factory, registry, or injected map near the boundary that reads the payment type. A small conditional is not automatically wrong; the goal is to keep changing provider behavior out of the stable checkout logic.

The shared contract must not erase real differences. Cash-on-delivery, asynchronous bank transfer, and immediate card authorization may have different states and failure models. Model those explicitly instead of forcing every method into a misleading boolean `process()`.

sections.title: Without Strategy — service owns a growing switch
With Strategy + Spring — context is dumb, map auto-grows
Payment Strategy — Who Does What
sections.content:
amber|PaymentStrategy|~The contract|one method: process|amount + details in|boolean out
blue|Concrete strategies|~Per gateway|CreditCardPayment, UPIPayment|each validates its own way|add gateway = add class
emerald|PaymentService (context)|~Delegates only|holds a strategy or map|no type checks inside|stays closed for change
violet|Selection|~Upstream choice|controller + factory/map|or Spring DI by bean name|never inside the service

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using only a boolean result**: payment flows often need states, provider references, retry meaning, and detailed failures.
- **Forcing different lifecycles together**: immediate authorization and cash on delivery may not satisfy one simple contract.
- **Putting provider implementation code in checkout**: keep changing integration details in the strategy.
- **Assuming selection vanishes**: a boundary still maps the requested method to an allowed implementation.
- **Sharing unsafe mutable strategy state**: injected singleton strategies must handle concurrent calls correctly.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Put genuinely interchangeable payment behavior behind a meaningful interface
- Keep provider selection near the input boundary or in a registry/factory
- The checkout workflow delegates without containing each provider's implementation
- A conditional is not automatically wrong; growing provider logic is the problem
- Do not force different payment lifecycles into a weak common result

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For a payment Strategy, I first define a contract that the payment methods actually share, including a useful request and result rather than only a boolean. For example, `PaymentStrategy.authorize(request)` can return an authorization ID and status; a card strategy calls its gateway while a UPI strategy starts its own provider flow. The checkout service delegates through that interface, while a small factory, registry, or injected map selects the implementation near the boundary that reads the requested type. This keeps changing provider code out of checkout and makes each strategy testable. I do not remove conditionals at any cost: cash on delivery or an asynchronous bank transfer may have different lifecycle states, so I model those differences instead of forcing them into a misleading common method.

question: How do you use Spring's @Qualifier annotation for Strategy pattern-style selection?
title: Strategy Pattern with Spring @Qualifier
direct_answer: When several beans implement one strategy interface, Spring can't autowire it alone — it throws **NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException**. Give each implementation a name and select it with **@Qualifier** for a fixed choice, or inject a **Map<String, Strategy>** that Spring auto-fills with every bean (keyed by bean name) for **runtime** selection.

sections.title: Spring-Powered Strategy Selection
sections.content:
Strategy naturally produces **many beans of one type** — three classes implementing `ShippingStrategy`, all annotated `@Component`. If a service just autowires `ShippingStrategy`, Spring can't decide which one and throws **NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException**.

Two fixes. For a **fixed** choice known at startup, use **@Qualifier("name")** on the injection point to name the exact bean. For a **runtime** choice from a known set, inject a **`Map<String, ShippingStrategy>`** — Spring populates it with every matching bean, keyed by bean name, and you look up the strategy by a string at request time.

Either way you've combined Strategy with dependency injection: no `new`, fully mockable in tests, and adding a strategy is just adding a `@Component`.

sections.title: Without DI — context hardcodes the strategy
With @Qualifier (fixed) and Map (dynamic)
Spring Strategy Wiring at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|The problem|~Many beans, one type|3 ShippingStrategy beans|plain autowire fails|NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
blue|@Qualifier|~Fixed selection|name on the injection point|wired once at startup|explicit and simple
emerald|Map injection|~Dynamic selection|Map<String, Strategy>|Spring fills by bean name|pick at runtime by key
violet|Why DI not new|~Container benefits|mockable in tests|managed lifecycle|add bean = add @Component

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`new StrategyImpl()` in the context.** Bypasses Spring entirely — no mocking, no lifecycle, no swapping. Always inject.
- **Qualifier on the class but not the injection point.** You must add `@Qualifier` where the bean is *consumed*, not only where it's defined, or Spring still can't disambiguate.
- **Assuming map keys.** The key is the *bean name*. With bare `@Component` it's the class name with the first letter lowercased (`expressShipping`), not `"express"`. A null lookup usually means a wrong key.
- **Forgetting `@Primary` exists.** When one implementation should be the default, mark it `@Primary` instead of qualifying every injection point.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Multiple beans of one type** make a bare autowire throw `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`.
- **@Qualifier("name")** picks a specific bean for a fixed, startup-time choice.
- **Map<String, Strategy>** is auto-filled by Spring for runtime selection by key.
- **Map keys = bean names** — default is the class name, first letter lowercased.
- **Never `new`** a strategy in the context — inject it for testability and lifecycle.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: When you use Strategy in Spring, you end up with several beans of the same type — say three classes implementing ShippingStrategy, all annotated at Component. If a service just autowires ShippingStrategy, Spring doesn't know which one to give it and throws a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. There are two clean fixes. The first is at Qualifier, for a fixed choice. You give each bean a name, then on the injection point — the constructor parameter — you add at Qualifier with the name you want, like express. Spring finds that exact bean and wires it once at startup. The second, and more powerful, approach is map injection for runtime selection. You declare a constructor parameter of type Map of String to ShippingStrategy. Spring automatically fills that map with every ShippingStrategy bean, using the bean name as the key. Now at runtime you do a map lookup with a string — like the shipping type the user chose — and call the strategy you get back. The key thing to know is that the map keys are bean names. If you write at Component with an explicit name like express, the key is express. If you just write at Component with no name, the key defaults to the class name with the first letter lowercased. A null lookup almost always means the key doesn't match the actual bean name. The big mistake is calling new ExpressShipping inside the service. That throws away everything the container gives you — you can't mock it in tests, you lose lifecycle management, and you can't swap implementations without editing code. Always inject. And if one implementation should be the default, mark it at Primary instead of qualifying every single injection point.

question: How is Strategy pattern different from simple polymorphism via inheritance?
title: Strategy Pattern vs Inheritance Polymorphism
direct_answer: Both inheritance and Strategy can use runtime polymorphism. Inheritance varies behavior by choosing a subtype and also creates an `is-a` relationship; Strategy gives a context a separate behavior object through composition. The context can replace that object when its design permits, and one behavior can be reused by unrelated contexts without expanding a class hierarchy.

sections.title: Inheritance vs Composition in Behavior Modeling
sections.content:
Inheritance and Strategy both dispatch behavior at runtime through polymorphism, so “compile time versus runtime” is not the real distinction.

With inheritance, a subtype overrides behavior as part of what the object *is*. A `SavingsAccount` may specialize `Account`, and the selected object's concrete subtype remains its type. With Strategy, a context *has* a separate behavior dependency, such as a `PricingPolicy`. The same context class can receive a different policy during construction or later if mutation is intentionally supported.

Composition avoids multiplying subclasses when several independent behaviors can vary. Inheritance remains useful for a stable substitutable type hierarchy. Strategy also adds another object and delegation layer, so use it when the behavior is meaningfully interchangeable.

sections.title: Strategy vs Inheritance
sections.content:
| Aspect | Inheritance (IS-A) | Strategy (HAS-A) |
|---|---|---|
| Behavior binding | Compile-time, in the hierarchy | Runtime, via injection/setter |
| Flexibility | Fixed once instantiated | Swappable any time |
| Combining behaviors | Needs many subclasses (N×M) | Compose/chain strategies (linear) |
| Code reuse | Shared base-class methods | Shared via the strategy contract |
| Testing | Instantiate a concrete subclass | Inject a mock strategy |
| Best when | Subclasses share real implementation | Behavior varies, structure stays same |

sections.title: Which One to Reach For
sections.content:
amber|Inheritance (IS-A)|~Behavior is identity|Dog barks because it IS a Dog|locked at construction|use for shared real code
blue|Strategy (HAS-A)|~Behavior is injected|car picks toll rule by day|swap at runtime|use when behavior varies
emerald|Binding time|~The deciding question|will it change after new?|yes -> Strategy|no, intrinsic -> inheritance
violet|Combining|~Many behaviors at once|subclasses explode (N x M)|strategies compose linearly|favor composition (GoF)

sections.title: Inheritance — behavior locked at construction
Strategy — behavior injected and composable
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling inheritance compile-time dispatch**: overridden instance methods are selected at runtime.
- **Assuming every Strategy is mutable**: a context may choose one strategy at construction and keep it.
- **Using inheritance without an `is-a` contract**: code reuse alone can create a fragile hierarchy.
- **Adding Strategy when behavior never varies**: composition has an extra object and delegation cost.
- **Ignoring shared implementation**: inheritance or a helper may still be useful when the subtype relationship is genuine.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Both designs can use runtime polymorphism
- Inheritance models a substitutable `is-a` type relationship
- Strategy composes a separate `has-a` behavior dependency
- A context may replace its strategy when the API intentionally supports it
- Composition helps independent behaviors vary without multiplying subclasses

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Inheritance and Strategy both use runtime polymorphism, so I would not describe inheritance as compile-time binding. Inheritance varies behavior through a subtype and represents an `is-a` relationship. Strategy gives a context a separate behavior object through composition. For example, an `OrderService` can receive a `PricingPolicy` without becoming a subtype of that policy, and the policy can be reused elsewhere. The context can swap policies if its API allows that, although many designs choose one at construction and keep it. I prefer inheritance for a stable substitutable hierarchy and Strategy when an independent behavior needs to vary or combine without creating many subclasses.
